nameStory: Despite its "Mexican" name, this bright flower is often confusingly called the "African marigold" in garden centers! The name Mexican marigold is actually more accurate - this cheerful plant is truly native to Mexico and Central America. The Aztecs called it cempaxochitl and treasured it for ceremonies, medicine, and decoration long before European explorers ever saw it.
description: Mexican marigold is a sturdy annual flower that creates impressive displays with its large, puffy blooms in shades of yellow, orange, and gold. These garden favorites grow anywhere from 8 inches to nearly 3 feet tall, with strong, branching stems that smell distinctly spicy when touched. The flowers are like pompoms made of countless tiny petals all packed together, creating those classic marigold heads that can be 2-4 inches across. While originally from Mexico, they're now grown worldwide as popular ornamental plants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, dense flower heads that feel like soft pompoms, typically 2-4 inches across in bright yellow, orange, or gold colors. Each 'flower' is actually made up of dozens of tiny individual flowers packed tightly together.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery leaves that are arranged alternately on the stem. When crushed, they release a strong, pungent smell that's distinctly spicy and somewhat citrusy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, sturdy plants that branch from the base, growing 8 inches to 3 feet tall. The stems are thick and succulent-feeling, with a smooth texture and light green color.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Long, thin, dark seeds with a papery tuft at one end that helps them disperse in the wind. They develop in the center of spent flower heads after blooming.

habitat: In New England, Mexican marigolds are found exclusively in cultivated settings like gardens, flower beds, and containers since they cannot survive our winters. They thrive in full sun locations with well-drained soil and are commonly planted as colorful annuals in both formal and informal garden settings.

seasonality.spring: Young plants appear in gardens after the last frost, usually late May or early June, as small green seedlings with their characteristic feathery leaves just beginning to develop.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant large, colorful flower heads from July through early fall. The plants reach their full height and spread during this time.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming until the first hard frost kills the plants, often providing color well into October. Seeds mature and can be collected for next year's planting.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely absent as they cannot survive freezing temperatures. Only dried seeds remain, either collected by gardeners or scattered naturally.

funFact: These marigolds are edible and are used to make a traditional Mexican tea called 'té de cempasúchil' - but more surprisingly, they're also used commercially to make chicken feed that creates more golden egg yolks and gives farmed salmon their pink color!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with French marigolds, but Mexican marigolds are much larger overall with bigger, fuller flower heads that feel more densely packed. Memory trick: 'Mexican = Maximum' - bigger plants, bigger flowers than their French cousins.
contextualKnowledge: The common name 'African marigold' is completely misleading since these plants are native to Mexico, not Africa. This confusion arose because they were first introduced to Europe through North African trade routes, leading to the mistaken geographic association that persists in many garden centers today.
compareHints: Mexican marigolds are significantly larger than French marigolds in every way - taller plants, bigger leaves, and much larger flower heads. While French marigolds tend to have more varied flower colors including deep reds and bi-colors, Mexican marigolds stick mainly to the yellow-to-orange spectrum. The flower heads of Mexican marigolds are also much more densely packed and pompom-like compared to the more open, daisy-like flowers often seen in French marigolds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: French marigolds are much more compact and delicate than Mexican marigolds, staying under a foot tall compared to their 1-3 foot cousins.
